Batteries charged in the cold fail more violently; a 33% solar cell; old clothes turned into energy storage; the energy radar.
TECH RADAR
Charging in the cold leaves batteries with a hidden weak spot
No. 13 · Tuesday 3 November 2026 · Energy · 6 min read
 
IN 30 SECONDS
1UK researchers filmed batteries from inside with high-speed X-rays: cells repeatedly charged below zero build up metallic lithium and, when they overheat, fail more violently, starting from the core.
2A German-led team reaches 33.25% efficiency with a solar cell that stacks perovskite on silicon, by smoothing the silicon's surface texture.
3Energy radar: research is flat and slowing this year, but new battery projects on GitHub more than tripled in a year while hydrogen projects nearly halved.
380
new energy papers today
33.25%
efficiency of today's perovskite–silicon tandem solar cell
+239%
new battery projects on GitHub, Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025
SIGNAL OF THE DAY
Why lithium-ion cells charged in the cold fail more violently
Journal of Power Sources · 31 October · Free PDF  Journal  High-impact journal
Who wrote it: Charles Kirchner-Burles and 13 others · National Physical Laboratory, The Faraday Institution, University College London (United Kingdom, Germany, France) · among the authors Paul Robert Shearing, h-index 94
Context. When a lithium-ion battery is charged below zero, part of the lithium does not slip inside the electrode as it should but settles on its surface as a thin layer of metal. This 'lithium plating' is a known risk for cars and devices used in cold climates. The most serious failure is 'thermal runaway': the cell overheats on its own, faster and faster, and can catch fire.
The team aged commercial high-power cylindrical cells by charging them repeatedly below freezing. Cells with a lot of plated lithium were less stable when heated, failed at lower temperatures and, once runaway started, did so in more violent and less predictable ways. Filming the inside with high-speed X-ray tomography showed that the failure always began near the centre of the rolled-up electrodes, where the winding is tightest and plating is worst. It is today's signal because winters with extreme cold are becoming more frequent, and the study points to a specific weak spot in cell design that manufacturers can address.
PAPERS OF THE DAY · ENERGY
Silicon solar cellsdeclining
Research share −29% in 3 years · 1,243 papers in 2025
What it is about. Almost all solar panels today are made of silicon, which is close to its efficiency limit. Placing a thin perovskite layer on top, a 'tandem' cell, captures more of the sunlight, but the two layers are hard to match.
Chemical Rounding Suppresses Morphology‐Induced Interfacial Losses in Perovskite–Silicon Tandem Solar Cells
Advanced Energy Materials · 31 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Nan Sun and 12 others · Forschungszentrum Jülich, University of Duisburg-Essen, Jülich Aachen Research Alliance (Germany, China, South Korea) · among the authors Christoph Josef Brabec, h-index 152
CONTEXTSilicon cells are etched with tiny pyramids to trap light, but a very thin perovskite layer cannot coat sharp pyramids evenly.
WHAT THEY DOThey make the pyramids smaller and then round their tips with an ozone-based chemical treatment, so the perovskite layer can follow the surface without gaps.
RESULTThe resulting tandem cell converts 33.25% of sunlight into electricity.
WHY IT MATTERSMatching the two layers is one of the obstacles to tandem panels on rooftops; this is a manufacturing-friendly fix.
Supercapacitor materialsstable
Research share −8% in 3 years · 7,994 papers in 2025
What it is about. Supercapacitors store energy on the surface of very porous carbon: they charge and release power in seconds. The more internal surface the carbon has, the better.
Upcycling Cotton–Polyester Textile Waste Into High Quality Biochar and Activated Carbon for Energy Storage Applications
Energy Technology · 31 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: Md Sumon Reza and 9 others · North Carolina State University (United States) · among the authors Fanxing Li, h-index 57
WHAT THEY DOThey heat waste fabrics (cotton, polyester and a 50/50 blend) without oxygen to turn them into carbon, then treat it to open up its pores, and test it as a supercapacitor material.
RESULTThe blend gives the most porous raw carbon; after treatment, cotton-derived carbon reaches 2,537 m² of internal surface per gram and stores 112 farads per gram, about twice the blend.
WHY IT MATTERSFast fashion produces mountains of mixed-fabric waste: turning it into energy-storage material is a simple circular-economy route.
Hybrid renewable energy systemsgrowing
Research share +41% in 3 years · 4,482 papers in 2025
What it is about. Ammonia (for fertilisers) and methanol (for plastics and fuels) are made today from natural gas. 'Green' versions use hydrogen from renewable electricity and CO2 captured from the air.
Transition to low-carbon ammonia and methanol through hybrid energy systems and direct air capture: A 4E assessment
Energy Reports · 31 October  Journal  High-impact journal  Free PDF ↗
Who wrote it: GholamReza Aghdami and 4 others · K. N. Toosi University of Technology, Niroo Research Institute (Iran) · among the authors Majid Amidpour, h-index 54
WHAT THEY DOComputer models compare four ways of making methanol and ammonia, from natural gas with or without carbon capture to fully green routes powered partly by a solar thermal plant, on technical, economic and environmental grounds.
RESULTThe gas-based routes are profitable (net present value of $285 million for methanol with carbon capture and $207 million for conventional ammonia), while green methanol and ammonia cost $856 and $837 per tonne and do not pay off at a 10% cost of capital.
WHY IT MATTERSGreen chemicals depend heavily on the cost of borrowing money: cheaper financing, not just better technology, is what tips the balance.
RADAR OF THE DAY · ENERGY
What it is about. How we produce, store and move energy: solar, wind, batteries, hydrogen, power grids and electric vehicles. It is the largest of the five verticals and the one most supported by public funding.
+2%
research share compared with 3 years ago
−10%
momentum this year compared with all research
28.2%
papers with declared public funding
Where research is growing (topic share, 2022→2025)
Advanced battery technologies
new chemistries and designs for longer-lasting, safer batteries
▲ +52%
Electric vehicles and infrastructure
electric cars and buses, charging and their real emissions
▲ +47%
Hybrid renewable energy systems
combining sun, wind, storage and hydrogen
▲ +41%
Smart grids and power systems
grids that balance supply and demand automatically; slowing this year
▲ +39%
What developers and the public do
SIGNALGITHUB
(year on year)		HACKER NEWS
(year on year)
«battery»▲ +239%▼ −9%
«smart grid»▲ +183%▼ −38%
«solar energy»▲ +120%▼ −27%
«hydrogen»▼ −48%▼ −16%
GitHub: new projects; Hacker News: stories discussed (few for smart grid, hydrogen and solar: 10 to 33 per quarter). Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025; for comparison, all new GitHub projects grew 62% and Hacker News discussions fell 38%. Wikipedia, 12 months: views down for energy storage (−29%), hydrogen economy (−37%), perovskite solar cells (−33%) and fusion power (−15%). Data updated 3 November.
In short: Developers keep pouring into batteries and smart grids, while hydrogen is the only signal shrinking, consistent with today's paper on the poor economics of green ammonia. In research, energy holds steady but slows this year.
WORDS OF THE DAY
h-index — a measure of how often a researcher is cited: an h-index of 50 means 50 papers cited at least 50 times each. Above 40 usually indicates an established name in the field.
Thermal runaway — a chain reaction in which a battery heats itself faster and faster until it vents gas or catches fire.
Lithium plating — metallic lithium settling on a battery electrode instead of entering it, typically when charging in the cold or too fast.
Tandem solar cell — two solar layers stacked on top of each other, each capturing a different part of sunlight.
WORTH WATCHING
Tomorrow the radar of the day is on LLMs and generative AI. Worth watching: whether battery makers change cell designs or charging rules for cold climates after findings like today's.
